speechtext:
I think that the hon. gentleman from Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) is to be congratulated on having brought to the attention of this House and of the country, by the Bill which he has introduced, a matter of very great importance and a matter which is of distinct public interest to the people of this country and particularly to the members of this House who are compelled to live in Ottawa for a considerable portion of every year. I think the Bill has special interest in view of the condition in which we find 'the water supply of Ottawa to-day, which is directly traceable to the fact that the water of the noble river that flows past these parliament buildings has been allowed for years to be polluted by the discharge of raw sewage into it. Everyone will agree with the hon. member in the idea that it is a very great misfortune and a matter of very great regret, that the rivers of this country have been allowed from the time of the earliest settlement of the country to be made receptacles for raw sewage untreated in any way. The danger arising from that is an ever increasing danger. A? the country grows and the pop-

ulation becomes greater the danger of pollution and the consequent danger to public health becomes greater. People- living along the banks of these streams have, in many oases, no other source of water supply than the streams and rivers which are polluted from the sewage of towns and villages further up these rivers. But while everybody would agree with the object which the hon. gentleman has in view, yet, at the same time, I think it would not be wise or desirable that, this legislature should pass any Bill without giving the most thorough and careful consideration n&t only to the conditions that make such legislation necessary but also to the great expense involved in remedying the existing evils. It would not do to pass any measure in such drastic terms as the Bill which the hon. gentleman has presented. In addition to that it is fair to bear in mind that while the first section of this Bill makes it an offence punishable by penalties to deposit or permit to be deposited any sewage or other refuse in any navigable stream, there are navigable waters into which sewage can be discharged without danger to the people living in the vicinity. For instance, if sewage is discharged into waters which are navigable but which are salt, the water not being fit to use for domestic purpose and where there is a tidal rise and fall, there is no menace or danger to the public health. Therefore I consider that a Bill of this kind must be considered with regard to all of these features, and exceptions would have to be made to meet cases like that. Then we must . also "bear in mind that for a very great many years towns and villages have been constructing sewage system under legislative authority authorizing them to discharge sewage into these navigable streams without treating it by means of septic tanks or otherwise so as to render it harmless. In those cases it must be borne in mind that a very large sum of money will have to be spent by many towns in this country in order to provide means for treating the sewage before it goes into the streams ot disposing of it in other ways. While that i3 not a consideration which should weigh against the great consideration of the public health of the country, yet, in dealing with the matter, it should be borne in mind that these expenditures have been incurred and any Bill for the prevention of further pollution of streams should be drafted in such a way as to bear with as little harshness as possible upon communities that have spent large sums on sewage systems of this kind. In many cases this sewage has been allowed to flow into navigable streams under an idea which very generally prevailed until comparatively Tecent years that running water would purify it-273i
self in a certain distance; in many cases the assumption was that sewage from towns and villages would purify itself in ten miles,, so that at that distance below a town or city the water would be so purified that noharm would be done by using it. That theory, like many old theories, has been exploded. It is now universally conceded by scientists that the only thing that will destroy bacteria is heat and while in the course of distance sewage and bacteria carried in it will be diffused, so that there-is less danger, the bacteria are still there' and if anyone using the water is unfortunate enough to come in contact with the typhoid bacillus which is caused by the depositing of sewage in streams, there is danger of contracting the disease with all the evil results that will follow. I have some figures here showing what the towns of Canada have done with regard to the disposal of their sewage. I do not propose to go into that very fully but I shall make brief reference to some cases. In Nova Scotia there are fourteen towns which are discharging their sewage into different waters. Most of them are discharging the sewage into waters of the ocean or into waters that are tributary to the ocean	and	which	cannot	be used
for domestic purposes. For instance, Dartmouth and Halifax discharge their sewage into Halifax harbour. I presume that the waters of Halifax harbour cannot be used for domestic purposes at all, and that at Halifax there is little danger or menace to the public health in the disposition of the sewage. Digby discharges its sewage into the Annapolis basin; Kentvill'e into the Cornwallis river -which is, I believe, a tidal river; Liverpool into the Mersey; Middleton into the Annapolis river'; Stellarton into the East river; Sydney into Sydney harbour; Windsor into the Avon, which is also a tidal river; and Truro into the Salmon river. In the province of Nova Scotia, I think very careful investigation into the facts would show-my hon. friends from Nova Scotia will know more about the matter than I do-that in nearly all those cases there is no menace to the public health because of raw sewage being discharged into the streams. In not a single case in the province of Nova Scotia is the sewage treated in any way before it is so discharged into the waters into which it goes. In Prince Edward Island, the sewage of Summerside is discharged into Bedeque bay. In New Brunswick, at Campbellton, the sewage is discharged into Baie des Chaleurs, at Chatham into the Miramichr river which is a tidal river. The waters-at Newcastle into which its sewage is discharged are not used for domestic purposes. Moncton discharges its sewage into the Petitcodiac river which is a tidal river and St. Andrews into the harbour. The city of

Fredericton discharges its sewage into the St. John river, and the city of St. John into the harbour.
Would all those towns, including Glace Bay, the sewage of which goes into Glace Bay harbour, come under the prohibition of this Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I believe that they would. I think there is no question about it, because it says that no person shall discharge sewage into any navigable water, or into any water that flows into any navigable water, and I think there is no doubt that those harbours are properly described as navigable waters. As I have said, Fredericton discharges its sewage into the river St. John, and that is true of other towns above the city of Fredericton. There is no doubt whatever that the discharge of raw sewage from Fredericton and the towns above that city polutes the waters of the St. John river, and is a menace to the people living below, who in some cases, owing to the peculiar formation of the country, are at certain seasons of the year absolutely and entirely dependent upon the waters of that river for water for domestic purposes. In no New Brunswick town does sewage appear to be treated in any way at all. Then in the province of Quebec there are thirty-seven towns, of which I have a list here, and which discharge their sewage into the waters of different rivers. Many of these towns discharge into rivers like the St. Lawrence, into the tributaries of the St. Lawrence, into the Richelieu and Massampi, the St. Francis, and other rivers and there is practically no treatment of the sewage in any case. The result is that the water of these rivers, in practically every case, cannot be used to-day for do-* mestic purposes with any safety without .first being treated for domestic purposes.
In the province of Ontario, there are fifty-two towns of which I have a list, and which discharge their sewage into the lakes and rivers, into such rivers, for instance, as the Detroit river, the Welland river, the St. Lawrence, the St. Clair, the St. Marys, the Rideau, the Ottawa and Rainy river, and of these fifty-two towns eleven treat their sewage by means of septic tanks and filtration beds and in other ways before it is placed in the water. In Manitoba, the province from which my hon. friend (Mr. Bradbury) who has moved this resolution comes, there are six towns that are disposing of their sewage. Brandon discharges its sewage into the Assiniboine, Carman into the Boyne river, Portage la Prairie into the Assiniboine, St. Boniface into the Red river. In the case of Souris, the river is not named, Winnipeg discharges into the Red river and Assiniboine river. In no [DOT]ease is the sewage treated, but I find in regard to Souris that it is proposed to put- in a filtration system. The provinces of Sas-Mr. HAZE NT
katchewan and Alberta seem to be rather ahead of the other provinces in this matter in that they are making provision, and in some cases have made provision for treating the sewage before it is discharged into the water. At Moosejaw, the sewage which runs into the Moosejaw creek is treated in septic tanks. Prince Albert discharges its sewage into the North basKatchewan river, and I have no record of any treatment of it. At Regina, there is treatment by means of septic tanks, sedimentation, disinfection tanks and biological filters. SasKatoon discharges its sewage into the South Saskatchewan river and has sewage disposal works under construction at the present time. In Alberta, Calgary discharges its sewage into the Bow river, Edmonton into the North Saskatchewan river, and part of the sewage of that city is treated in septic tanks. Lethbridge discharges into the Belly river and there a sewage purification plant is to be installed at once. The sewage of McLeod goes into the Old Man river, and nothing is said about treating me sewage there. Medicine Hat discharges into the South Saskatchewan river; and has a sewage plant under consideration. Red Deer discharges into the Red Deer river and has a purification plant under consideration. Wetaski-win discharges into Bigstone creek and is proposing to erect sewage disposal works. In British Columbia, there are septic tanks at Kamloops which discharges into the Thompson river. Nelson discharges into the Kootenay river. New Westminster into the Fraser river, Prince Rupert into the Pacific ocean, Rossland into Trail creek and Vancouver into the Pacific ocean. In none of these cases is there any arrangement far. the treatment of the sewage, and I fancy in many of them there is no necessity for such treatment. In considering the terms of a Bill of this kind it is clear that very great care will have to be taken not to do injustice to the communities which have gone to the expense of arranging for the disposal of their sewage and which are treating it in a way that does not constitute a menace to the health of the community. If f'arliament decides that no Taw sewage shall be placed in those rivers or waters where it will be a menace to the health of the community, the cost of changing the system that now exists in many of those towns and cities will be very large indeed. I have some figures here, and it will take only a few moments to give them to the House. Respecting the cost of treatment, the town of Berlin in the province of Ontario which has an approximate population of 10,000, treats its sewage in septic tanks. After treatment the effluent is pumped up fifty feet to natural sand beds, whence it passes downwards through the sand, the water reappearing at a lower level as l springs. The filtrate thug obtained is per-

fectly clear and odourless, and in appearance cannot be distinguished from spring water. The volume of sewage has now reached 700,000 gallons per twenty-four hours, and the filtering material is not sludged up in the slightest degree. The plant 'was designed for the present population of 10,000 with allowances for extensions sufficient to handle the sewage of three times the present population. Berlin is an inland town and is situated on a small stream that has a very small summer flow. The actual cost of stream filtration works was $45,750 or in round figures between $4 and $5 per head of the population of the town. 1 am told that the plant is regarded by sanitary engineers as one of the most efficient plants in the Dominion. (Reading):
As indicating the cost to a small municipality, the town of Palmerston may be cited. I he cost for population of 2,000 was estimated at $15,900. Of this amount, $2,200 was es-ti mated cost of drain to the Maitland river, due to the peculiar topography of the locality, and constitutes an item that would not be involved in a great majority of cases. Deducting this unusual item, gives a cost of $13,-<00 or, say, $7 per head of population. In explanation of the cost, it should also he stated that it is proposed to give a complete treatment in a plant provided that both sprinkling filters and septic tanks.
For small municipalities, with very limited financial resources, a sewage treatment with a revolving screen to remove the solids, and, subsequent sterilization with hypochlorite, could probably he installed at a cost of about $3 per head of population. It should he a separate system

That is there should be a system for the sewage from bouses and also a system for the sewage from the streets.
It should he a separate system to avoid the necessity of handling storm water. This would ensure a fairly constant flow and thus avoid radical changes at short intervals in the amount of hypochlorite used.
Por a large city, the experience of Baltimore shows that a very complete system, providing for (1st) rapid sedimentation; (2nd) sprinkling filter, and, (3rd) secondary sedimentation, can he provided for about $6 per head of population.
In Montreal, where the papulation, I believe, is about 600,000, it would cost $6 per head, or about $3,600,000.
The Baltimore plant also provides for a fourth treatment with hypochlorite. This, however, is perfectly unnecessary, hut is used to guard against any possible infection of the eery valuable oyster beds below the city. I
I do not for one moment wish to argue that the cost is in any way prohibitive or that it should deter this Parliament, if it is believed to he in the general interest of Canada to do so, from passing legislation that would have the effect of causing the purification of the rivers and streams
throughout the country upon which the people have in very .many oases, if not in nearly all cases, to depend for water for drinking and domestic purposes.

May I ask
the hon. gentleman if he has at any time considered the matter of the jurisdiction of this Parliament even over navigable rivers in regard to this Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No, I do not profess to
have made any careful study of the question, but it seems to me that, if it is a matter affecting the general health of the people of the country, it might be fully within our jurisdiction. We might almost deal with it perhaps from the standpoint, speaking offhand, of the navigation of the country because, surely it is not in the interest of navigation that- the rivers and streams should he polluted in this way byraw sewage. However, that is a matter to be considered. There is no doubt that the provinces have jurisdiction over the streams within their boundaries from the standpoint o>f public health and from other standpoints. This is a matter that has been discussed in this House before and it has been discussed in the Senate where-Senator Beloourt has introduced a Bill during the present session to which I shall refer in a few moments. The impression seems to have prevailed in the House that there was jurisdiction in this Parliament to enact a Bill that would affect the whole country. But I do not wish to discuss that phase of the matter now.
I was saying that even iiif the cost is large, and the cost would undoubtedly be large, as it would run into millions of dollars, that would not be a reason foT failing to pass such legislation if the interests of the country demand it. But there are many communities throughout the country that would undoubtedly feel that they were being perhaps dealt with in a somewhat arbitrary way if they were to be compelled to change tjieir whole sewage system and go to a large expense in order to he able to say that the sewage, when it goes into the streams, goes in such a way that it will not do barm, or adapt "Ome other system altogether. Still, at the same time, the public health and the public interest are superior to any consideration of that sort and if Parliament decides that, it has power to deal with the matter and. that the health of the country is very seriously affected, as I believe it is, by -the discharge of raw sewage into these streams, then the financial consideration should not deter Parliament from taking action. But, before legislating or dealing with the question, we should have before this Parliament .more accurate information than we have at the present time and there-

fore it i3 my intention to move that this question shall be referred to a select committee for the purpose of considering the matter and reporting back to the House. I douibt if anything can be accomplished this year, but a commencement might be made and as the effect of bringing this matter before the House will undoubtedly be to direct attention to it and cause discussion throughout the country during the recess, perhaps at the next session the matter may he dealt with in a way that will be for the nublic good.
The present Bill, I think, would have to be modified in a number of respects. The first section refers to the discharge of sewage in all navigable streams and -waters. As I have pointed out, there would have to be very considerable exceptions made in regard to that. Then, in regard to the third section of the Bill, it provides that:	,	.
Where, at the date of the passing of this Act, any sewage or matter referred to in subsection 1 of section 1 of this Act flows into any navigable water, or into any other water which flows into any navigable water, this Act shall, in the case of municipal corporations, come into force two years after it is assented to by the Governor General.
At the end of two years from the time this Bill is assented to by the Governor in Council, section 1 will be operative in so far as municipal corporations are concerned, and it would be unlawful to discharge sewage into any navigable waters. Having regard to the amount of work which will be necessary for each town to undertake to change the system of sewage, I think it will be admitted that two years is entirely too short a time. It would be preferable, if we were dealing with that matter, to adopt section 4 of the Senate Bill which was introduced by Senator Belcourt this year. It provides that:
The Governor iu Council may make such regulations, general or special, as are requisite or expedient to carry out the purposes and intent of this Act; and the said regulations shall have force and effect as of and from the date of the publication thereof in the Canada Gazette.
2.	The minister may appoint such officers as ihe deems necessary to carry out and enforce the provisions of this Act, and may also designate any existing board of health or sanitary authority, or other person, for such purposes.
3.	The minister may make such orders and grant such permits as are provided for in such regulation.
This would give the Bill an elasticity which it does mot at all possess under clause 3, because the success or failure of an Act of this sort must depend upon the sane and sensible administration of it, and 1 do not think that the object can be attained by any legislation that is as drastic as that proposed by the present Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext:
May I be allowed, Mr. Speaker, to make one or two observations? With the principle of this Bill I do not disagree, but I do most strenuously object to the city of Ottawa being held up as a horrible example upon which to base this legislation. The hon. member for Selkirk has, I am afraid, not made a study of the reports of the many experts whom the city of Ottawa has engaged from time to time to ascertain the cause of the contamination of the water supply and to suggest a remedy. I am safe in saying that the two typhoid epidemics in this city were due to specific causes. It has been shown conclusively, I believe, that neglect on the part of those responsible for our intake pipe was the proximate cause of both epidemics. It has been established that our intake pipe was damaged by logs and the water being low and fire pressure being necessary, it was found, upon opening certain valves to get sufficient pressure, that sewage in the river was allowed to get into the pipe which supplied the pipe for domestic purposes, thereby causing the epidemic. It is a remarkable fact that the city of Hull, lying adjacent to the city of Ottawa, and on the other side of the river, has been using the Ottawa river water, without anv treatment, and has not experienced an epidemic, notwithstanding the fact that the town of Aylmer, I believe, disposes of its sewage into the river. The city of Ottawa, as I have indicated, is not responsible except in the sense of possible neglect on the part of those who were in charge of the laying of the intake pipe in not protecting it from being damaged. The city of Ottawa has taken steps to purify its water supply. It first brought here Mr. Hazen, a gentleman who is supposed to be the,, best expert on the continent in such matters. He suggested the expenditure of a large
sum of money and the establishment of a filtration plant. That suggestion was rejected by the people of Ottawa and the city then brought from England two of the leading experts in the world, who have made an examination of the condition of the Ottawa river and the surrounding country with the result that this session legislation will be asked to enable the city to take its water supply from the Gatineau lakes. The expenditure for this purpose will amount to several million dollars and the work is to be undertaken on the advice of Sir James Binnie. The best expert opinion is that we should take our water supply from the Gatineau lakes. There is no question that the Ottawa river is to a certain extent, like every other river, contaminated. It has been felt by the citizens of Ottawa and the city council that we should expend this large sum of money in order to ensure pure water for the city of Ottawa and the surrounding district. I make these observations in order to assure the House and the hon. gentleman who has last spoken (Mr. Sinclair) that the city of Ottawa is taking every possible step to ensure a supply of pure water.
Do you think they will take a step in our lifetime?

I think so. The result of
the lamentable epidemics that we had here has been to awaken the city council and those in authority to spare no effort to ensure a supply of pure water.
Are they still going to take the water from the Ottawa river?

.No. The idea is to take the water entirely from these lakes and to bring it here at an expenditure of several million dollars. We have to come to this Parliament for authority, as we are going into another province. The Bill will be introduced in a day or two, and I trust it will receive the assent of the House so that the work may be undertaken at the earliest possible moment.

I beg
to thank most sincerely my hon. friend from Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) and the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) for having dealt with this question in the manner they have done this evening. As a resident of Ottawa, I am bound to say that I do not share the optimistic view of my hon. friend from Ottawa (Mr. Fripp) as regards the action of the municipal authorities. I charge the municipal government of Ottawa with criminal negligence for the last five or six years. They are held responsible for the epidemics which have taken place in the city and which have caused the death of so many children. It is a well known fact.

that the taxpayers of Ottawa are subjected to-day to a double tax. I am asking myself if a test ease should not be made as to whether a poor man like your humble servant should be called upon to pay for pure water and for impure water at the same time. This brings before the public the broad question oft whether or not the city of Ottawa should' be made a federal district.
Or move the Capital.

As I am a property owner here, I would not say that; but really the municipal government of this city has not been up to the mark for the last five or six years, and the question of pure water in this city has given the Capital of the Dominion a bad name not only in Canada but throughout the world. It was not necessary-I say so frankly-to bring distinguished experts from England in order to know that our water was impure. Any Canadian expert might have said the same thing. I am glad to hear that the municipal government intend to get the water of the city from the Gatineau lakes, but I am asking myself if the taxpayers should be obliged to pay for the enormous expenditure since, for the last five or six years they have been subjected to a double tax. It costs me at least one hundred dollars a year to get pure water besides paying my water rates to the city. It is an incubus on the citizens. The municipal government should not be allowed to collect that tax from the citizens. It would be far better if we should decide once for all whether or not the capital should be made a federal district as it is in the United States. What the federal Government does in Ottawa in the way of improvements is above board. Under the old Administration and under the present one the commission for beautifying the capital of the Dominion has been and is doing splendid work. I congratulate my hon. friend from Argenteuil (Mr. Perley) on his policy in this matter. I know he is a friend of the Capital. I would ask him on behalf of the city of Ottawa to try to convince has colleagues in the Government thiat they should take over the city and make a federal district of it.

The fact that the health
branch of the public service has been assigned to the department over which I have the honour of presiding, is an excuse for my saying a few words on this subject that has been brought up by my hon. friend from Selkirk. I do not think anybody in this House is likely to underrate the importance of this subject, even, Mr. LEMIEUX.
if we had mot, as we have, had it painfully and deeply impressed upon us by the unfortunate epidemic in Ottawa which has been referred to and which has been experienced by any of us who have been here for the last four or five years. I do not propose to discuss that except to say that it must be with a feeling of hopeful relief that everybody recognizes that something at last is being done to make Ottawa the place that it should be, and that it has not been for the last few years. Something was said by my hon. friend from Selkirk, to whom this House owes a debt of thanks for bringing up this subject, as to the financial value of the human life that was sacrificed in connection with the various typhoid epidemics. That, however, is the least portion of the damage resulting from them. The far greater value of human life and the resultant good in arousing not only the civic but the national conscience on this subject makes a discussion of this kind very important:
Something has been said about the jurisdiction of this Parliament in connection with a Bill of this nature. As far as I have looked into the matter, my own mind is perfectly clear that this Parliament would have jurisdiction to deal with questions of this character. Section 92, clause 7 of the British North America Act, which deals With health matters, says:
The establishment, maintenance, and management of hospitals, asylums, charities and eleemosynary institutions in and for the province, other than marine hospitals.
That is practically all it has to say on health matters. It is only by use and wont that there has grown up in Canada a sort of legend, or practice at all events, that all health matters have been dealt with by the various municipal and .provincial bodies. My own feeling has long been that, as far as jurisdiction goes, this Parliament has very much greater power than the average man in the street thinks it has in regard to .health matters.
The Minister of Marine and Fisheries has pointed out quite forcibly some of the objections that would naturally be taken to the scope of this Bill. I think the hon. member who introduced the Bill would be himself the first to admit that the details of the Bill might not be workable, and that there would have to be very radical alterations and amendments. He was concerned not so much with the details as with the principle involved in the Bill, as a sound one and one of immense importance not only to the House but to the country; and, if that principle is .applied in this Bill or in some other Bill as a result, he will be doing excellent service to the country by bringing the subject to the attention of the House.

A very good way to work out this whole matter is, as has been suggested by my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, to refer the Bill to a committee who shall have power to summon witnesses and obtain evidence, so that this House before it takes action will have such information before it as will ensure that any step taken will be an absolutely wise and sound one.
Mr. W. F. CARROLL (South Cape Breton) I am glad the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries has moved an amendment that this Bill be referred to a select committee of this House. Coming from the province which I do, I would take objection to the first clause of the Bill as it stands, and would suggest that the committee appointed to deal with this matter should give a great deal of consideration to the first clause. The navigable waters referred to in the Bill must include the sea, bays, navigable rivers, and any waters upon which vessels sail. A great many of the towns in the province of Nova Scotia are seaports, and the sewage from these towns empties into the sea, or into the harbours and thence into the sea. I do not think anyone will seriously contend that the health of tie community is seriously endangered by the sewage being allowed to flow into the harbours, where the tide rises . and falls, or into the sea, as is the case in many Nova Scotia towns. In the town of Glace Bay, the sewage empties into the sea; in the town of Sydney, it empties into Sydney harbour, and in the towns of North Sydney and Sydney Mines the sewage flows into the sea. That is one reason why I am glad the Bill will be sent to. a select committee, and I hope they will take that into consideration, and exempt these places from the operation of such a Bill as this. I would direct the attention of hon. gentlemen of this House to this part of section 1:	' any other water that flows
into any navigable water.' There is a serious doubt in my mind as to whether or not this Parliament has jurisdiction to allow these words to sthnd in the Bill. We have jurisdiction, of course, so far as legislation in regard to navigable waters is concerned, but I think serious objection can be raised in respect to this portion of the Bill, even if this Parliament has power to pass a general law in this regard for the welfare of the people of Canada.

I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) in bringing this matter before the House, and to congratulate the members of this House upon having an opportunity to deal with this important subject. I do not think the city of Ottawa should receive the condemnation which it has received here to-night from certain members of this House. If it is
not creditable to the city of Ottawa that the water is in the condition that it is now and has been for some time past, then this Parliament is the last body of men that ought to say one word in regard to the pollution of water in the city of Ottawa, ot to cast any discredit' upon the citizens for not having attended to the matter. Hon. gentlemen of this House must be aware of the fact that typhoid fever is a preventable disease; that it is a disease capable of being carried and transmitted by water, and that sewage dumped into the rivers must pollute them. Knowing these facts, and yet having never undertaken to stop the pollution of streams, 1 say we are the last persons in the world to extend any criticism, and, if any persons in the Dominion of Canada should be obliged to drink contaminated water, they ought to be the members of this House. What was the argument of the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux)? He says the municipal government of Ottawa is guilty of criminal negligence because, as a result of not supplying the people of this city with pure water, numbers of its citizens have died from a preventable disease. If then, the corporation of the city of Ottawa is guilty of criminal negligence in not providing pure water for its citizens, the members of this Parliament are equally guilty of criminal negligence in not having taken any action with regard to the purifying of streams in various parts of the country.
Is it not the duty of the city of Ottawa to provide pure water for its citizens, who pay for it?

I am not exonerating the city of Ottawa; I am not saying that the city has done what it should-on the contrary I say the. city of Ottawa has not done what it should. But I do submit that if the city of Ottawa is open to condemnation on that ground, then the members of this Parliament are open to the same condemnation, for, having been possessed of a full knowledge as to what the pollution of streams really meant, we have allowed that pollution to go on without taking any action to stop it, and have sat here for weeks discussing matters not in any degree as important as the matter of the purification of streams. The hon. member for Rouville expressed himself as being glad that the city of Ottawa was to get its water from the Gatineau lakes. The hon. Minister of Agriculture, I think, took the same view, but neither the hon. member for Rouville nor the hon. Minister of Agriculture said anything as to what should be done with the sewage of the city of Ottawa. They were both concerned as to where the water supply should come from, but they said not one word as to where the

city should dump its sewage. Their argument was that because they live in the city of Ottawa and have to drink the water, the city should be sure to get its water-supply from a pure source; it does not matter ,so much where they dump the sewage. The hon. member for Rouville has to pay double taxes. I am glad he has to pay double taxes, because when a person's pocket is affected it is liable to make him think, and that payment of double taxes may cause the hon. gentleman to apply to this matter the ability and energy which he certainly possesses. The creation of Ottawa into a federal district was referred to. For what object? In order that we in this little portion of the Dominion may get pure water; we may spend any amount of money in making certain that we will .get pure water and then we will fold our arms and let the rest of the country look out for themselves.
Let me give one instance to show the manner in which typhoid is communicated, and how very important it is that even the smaller streams should be looked after and should be kept pure. A few years ago, ten or twelve years, on the wooded hillsides of the Alleghenies, a man was taken ill with typhoid. He had gone into that district, he -was taken ill and was confined in a house about fifty feet distant from a mountain stream which passed down and into the Susquehana river. Mile after mile the river pursued its course without coming near another dwelling which might pollute it, until it passed by the small town of Plymouth in Pennsylvania, a town of eight thousand population. The water supply of that town had always been considered pure, it had been derived for years from this river rising in the hills. The body wastes from this patient in this cottage on the bank of the mountain stream were thrown out in the winter on the snow. Nothing happened until spring but when the mild weather came the body wastes were washed down into the mountain stream and carried for miles until it came to this little town of eight thousand population. The first case of typhoid was noticed in the early part of April. At the end of a -week new cases were occuring at the rate of from fifty to one hundred a day until one-eighth of the population of that little town was affected. There were 1,104 cases and 114 deaths. The cost for sick bills and loss of earnings was estimated at about $97,000 while the loss through the death of -wage earners was estimated at about one-half a million dollars. This a short case and serves to illustrate a good many points in connection with the argument advanced by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury). The matter -was traced back so that there could be no possible doubt of it to that one case in the little cottage on the Mr. EDWARDS.
hillside. That illustrates very clearly how this disease is communicated and I declare that no legislation has ever been brought before this House which is more deserving of the earnest consideration of every member in this House than the Bill now before us. Some of the objections raised by the Minister of Marine were, I think, not very weighty. Of course in such cases as he has mentioned in the maritime provinces where sewage is deposited in salt water, the danger of causing typhoid is comparatively slight. The other objection which he pointed out I think could be got over. His idea of referring the Bill to a committee is a good one. That committee should call expert evidence from any part of Canada or from the United States which will add to our information and enable us to deal properly with this subject. The matter of cost to the towns and cities in disposing of their sewage is something which the towns and cities will have to bear. It is a question of right. Has a town which is getting its water supply from the upper part of a stream from a pure source any right to dump its own sewage into that river and contaminate the water which is being used lower down? No person in his senses will claim any such thing. The towns should provide a proper system for the disposal of sewage, even if it does cost money. However hon. gentlemen may regard this matter, and I believe they regard it as serious, we have not regarded it seriously enough in the past or we would have done someth.ng and I venture to say that there will yet come in Canada a generation which will look back on this and previous generations who have sat in this Parliament and allowed this matter to go by default and will think not very creditably of us in regard to it. It is a subject of extreme importance, and I shall give the Bill my very hearty support.

Mr. Speaker, the discussion that has taken place so far is evidence of a measure of interest in and appreciation of the importance of the Bill. I do not think, however, that in what has been said so far there has been a full appreciation of the magnitude of the question or of the task of dealing with it. If there was a possibility that by any legislation of this House we could abolish the evil to which this Bill alludes, this House has been criminally negligent in not having provided such legislation long ago. But 1 think it will strike anybody that it is not possible for this great evil to be met merely by legislation on the part of this Parliament. There are questions of juridiction and of responsibility and there are, above all, questions of expenditure-enormous expenditure-in order that this matter may

be dealt with; and there is still further the question as to what is the best means of dealing with it. The action of the hon. member in bringing the matter to the attention of the House by means of a Bill is entirely to be commended. I think that the proposal of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to refer the Bill to a committee for consideration is probably the next step properly to be taken. But let me suggest that there will have to be co-operation between this Government and Parliament and the legislatures and governments of the various provinces and the municipal organizations that are immediately and, directly affected. There will have to be co-operation between all these bodies if the object of the Bill is to, be achieved. There will have to be an agreement as to what is the best means of meeting the difficulty. There will have to be some arrangement as to financing, and as to the distribution of authority generally and of cost. I do not think that the work can be entered upon too soon, and the committee which is to be appointed will do well to give the matter their very best attention. The Government itself will do well to take up the matter with a view of secur-: ing co-operation with the provincial legislatures and municipalities, so as to achieve the result aimed at.
It struck me when the matter was 'being discussed that if the Dominion is able and willing to assume a share of the burdens of the various provinces in the matter of aid to agriculture or of aid to highways, this matter is of so much greater importance and so much more pressing than even the matter of highways or of aid to agriculture, that I would be willing to see the proposals which are now before the House as part of the policy of this Government in regard to aiding agriculture and improving highways withdrawn for the moment and the money proposed to be devoted to those purposes diverted to this tremendous and pressing question of the pollution of streams, with a view to protecting the public health. If we have money to spend in aid of highways and of agriculture, we may still better spend money in connection with the more pressing matter of the preservation of public health. I would like to see the Government of the day ,go beyond the appointment of a committee of the House, and introduce some policy that would look towards the adequate dealing with this very pressing and very important question. It is a question in regard to which the initiative might very well be taken and a large share of the burden undertaken by this Government and this Parliament.

Without desiring to trespass on the time of the House I would like to
make one or two remarks largely rising out of the remarks of the hon. member for Edmonton and the hon. member for Fron-tenac. As I listened to this interesting discussion it seemed to me to take on a broader scope particularly in relation to what fell from the hon. member for Edmonton. As I understand the common law with regard to the rights of people past whose property a stream flows, there is an indubitable right in every riparian proprietor to have the waters which flow past his property unimpaired in quality and undiminished in quantity. The courts of England are filled with cases in which corporations, public bodies, asylums, and municipal governments have been restrained from discharging their sewage into rivers, and the courts of Canada are also filled with such cases. It has been laid down as a cardinal principle that no person, corporation or institution, has any legal right to discharge into any stream in any British possession, that I am aware of, any deleterious matter that will appreciably contaminate it. The Ontario courts are filled with cases in which municipalities doing that sort of thing have been restrained by injunction.	As a Canadian proud
of the broad acres, expansive rivers, and fertile fields of my country, I have often felt that it was a crying shame that the natural heritage of the people, the streams of the country, should be contaminated by careless projection of deleterious matter into them. In this city I remember a case which went to the Supreme Court, the case of Rattey and Booth, a case well known to legal gentlemen, which had to do with the throwing of sawdust into the river. Some individual took an action against the men who were discharging the sawdust and they were restrained, and mulcted in damages, and if I remember correctly, when it came to a question of who should pay the damages, the court said, settle it among yourselves, you have all been guilty of wrong doing. If there is a town on the Ottawa river or on any stream which has a municipal system projecting into the stream and appreciably contaminating the waters, the citizens of that town, as I understand the law, are not liable, but the municipality which furnishes the sewage system is liable, and I have no doubt that the city of Ottawa or any other town would be liable.
With regard to the question of how best to deal with the matter, it seems so that in order to have the best effect there should be co-operation between the corporations and the Dominion. In that way the educative value would be great. There may be joint action involving federal legislation and, contemporaneously with it and in harmony with it, legislation by all t'he provinces having within their confines large commercial centres, which have found it very difficult to treat sewage properly owing

to the conditions arising out of industrial life. I agree with the hon. member for Edmonton in saying that the scope of the investigation ought to be enlarged in that way and for this reason also, that the jurisdiction of the provinces is different from that of the federal Parliament and there might arise certain circumstances in regard to streams running into navigable waters from one province to another which would require to be treated by legislation of the provinces quite separately from the legislation of the federal Parliament dealing with navigable streams. With other members (who have spoken, I think that the thanks of the House are due to the my hon. friend from Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) for bringing this question up, and I hope that the committee when appointed will give it a thorough drag-netting. Not only in Ottawa but all over the Dominion, we should so educate public opinion that the people will be made to realize that it is a serious crime to pollute the waters that the public need for their daily use.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time.
